lessons.title: What a QMS is and why regulated companies run one
lessons.summary: You will be able to explain what a quality management system is, name its core processes, and say which rules shape it for devices and for medicines.
lessons.why: In a medical device or pharma company almost every piece of work leaves a quality record behind: a signed procedure, a training record, a test result, a complaint, a change request. If you build a tool, a report or an AI assistant that reads or writes any of these, you are working inside the quality management system whether you planned to or not. Knowing how the system is built tells you who must approve your work, which records you may not change, and why the quality team asks the questions it asks.

p: A quality management system (QMS) is the documented, controlled way a company makes sure its products meet requirements and are safe for the people who use them. It is not one piece of software. It is a set of rules the company writes for itself (policies and procedures), the people trained to follow them, and the records that prove they were followed.

Regulators and customers cannot watch every product being made. Instead they check the system. If the system is sound and the records show it was followed, they can trust the output. That is why auditors ask to see procedures and records, not just the product.

Most QMS documentation forms a pyramid. At the top is a short quality policy and a quality manual that say what the company commits to. Below that are procedures (often called SOPs, standard operating procedures) that say who does what. Below those are work instructions and forms for specific tasks. At the bottom are records: the filled-in forms, test results and signatures that prove the work happened.
Documents describe what should happen. Records prove what did happen. A procedure can be revised; a record, once made, must not be changed without a trace.
list: Document control: every procedure has an owner, a version, an approval and an effective date, and only the current version is in use.
Training: people are trained on the procedures for their role before they do the work, and the training is recorded.
CAPA (corrective and preventive action): problems such as complaints, failed tests and audit findings are investigated to the root cause and fixed so they do not come back.
Change control: changes to products, processes, equipment or software are assessed, approved and recorded before they are made.
Internal audit: the company checks itself against its own procedures and the rules it must follow.
Management review: senior leaders regularly look at quality data and decide what to fix or fund.

p: A QMS does not treat every task the same. The effort a company spends on a process should match the risk that process carries for the patient and the product. A change to a label that tells a nurse the dose gets more review than a change to the colour of a box. A spreadsheet that calculates batch results needs more checking than one used to plan a team lunch.

This idea runs through all the main standards. For medicines, ICH Q9 describes quality risk management. For devices, ISO 14971 describes product risk management and ISO 13485 asks for a risk-based approach to the processes of the QMS itself. For you, it means the first question about any new tool is: what could go wrong for a patient or a product if this tool is wrong?

sections.h: The rules for devices and for medicines
p: For medical devices, ISO 13485 is the international standard for a QMS. In the United States, the FDA rule is 21 CFR Part 820. The FDA amended Part 820 into the Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference and took effect on 2 February 2026. In plain words, a device maker selling in the US now builds its QMS around ISO 13485 plus the extra FDA requirements kept in the rule.

For medicines, the legal rules in the US are the current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) regulations, such as 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211 for finished drugs. ICH Q10 is an international guideline that describes a pharmaceutical quality system across the product lifecycle. It names four elements: process performance and product quality monitoring, CAPA, change management, and management review. It names two enablers: knowledge management and quality risk management.

The two worlds use different words, but the core processes are the same: control documents, train people, fix problems at the root, control change, check yourself, and have leadership look at the data.

sections.h: What this means when you build something
p: If your tool creates or changes a quality record, that record must stay trustworthy: who did what and when must be clear, and old values must not silently disappear. If your tool is used to make a quality decision, such as whether a complaint must be reported, the tool itself usually has to be validated, meaning tested and documented to show it does what it is meant to do for that use.

An AI assistant does not change these rules. If it drafts a CAPA investigation, a trained person still owns and signs the result. If its prompt or model changes, that is a change to a validated tool and goes through change control. Plan for the quality team as a partner from day one, not as a final gate.

example.title: Worked example: one complaint moving through the QMS (example scenario)
p: Imagine a company that makes a reusable blood pressure cuff. A hospital reports that a cuff's air tube cracked after a few weeks. Follow the complaint through the system and notice how many QMS processes it touches.
None of these steps is unusual. This is the system doing its job: one problem leaves a trail of linked records that an auditor can follow from complaint to fix.
list: Complaint handling: a trained person logs the complaint in the complaint system, using the current version of the complaint procedure.
Risk and reporting: the team checks the product risk file to judge whether the crack could harm a patient and whether the event must be reported to the regulator.
CAPA: the investigation finds the tube material becomes brittle after repeated cleaning. A CAPA is opened to fix the root cause.
Change control: switching to a new tube material is a design and supplier change. It is assessed, tested, approved and recorded before production uses it.
Document control and training: the drawing, the supplier specification and the incoming inspection instruction are revised, approved, and the affected people are trained.
Management review: the trend of tube complaints and the CAPA status appear in the next management review so leaders can see the problem was closed.

practice.title: Trace a problem through the QMS
practice.goal: See how one quality event links the core QMS processes together.
steps: Pick a simple product you know, such as a kettle, a glucose meter or a pill bottle.
Write one realistic problem a customer could report about it.
On paper or in a spreadsheet, list each QMS process the problem would pass through: complaint handling, risk check, CAPA, change control, document control, training, management review.
For each process, write the record it would leave behind and who would sign it.
Ask Claude to review your list and point out any process or record you missed, then decide which suggestions are right.
practice.done_when: You have a table with at least six rows, each naming a QMS process, the record it creates and the role that approves it.

pitfalls: Thinking the QMS is a software product. The software only holds records; the system is the procedures, the trained people and the evidence.
Changing or deleting a record to fix a mistake. Corrections must be traceable, with the original value, the new value, who changed it and why.
Treating every task with the same effort. Match the depth of review and testing to the risk to the patient and product.
Bringing the quality team in at the end. Ask early which procedures your work falls under and what evidence they will need.

Leave the wrong value so that nothing is ever changed

The quality manual
A work instruction for setting up a filling machine

Tell the users about the new prompt in a team chat message
Wait for the next internal audit to mention it
Run it through change control as a tool change

lessons.title: Document control, training and records
lessons.summary: You will be able to follow a procedure from draft to retirement, link training to the version people actually used, and say what makes a record trustworthy on paper and in software.
lessons.why: Most tools an FDE builds in a regulated company read or write controlled documents and records: a search over SOPs, a dashboard of overdue training, a form that captures batch data. If the tool shows a superseded procedure, loses an audit trail or lets someone sign for work they were not trained to do, it creates a compliance problem instead of solving one. This lesson gives you the rules those tools must respect.

sections.h: The running case for this course
p: Every lesson in this course reuses one synthetic record set so you can see how the QMS processes connect. The records and IDs are invented for training. Two cases run side by side because device makers and medicine makers use slightly different words for the same ideas.
MedTech case: a company makes a reusable blood pressure cuff. Pharma case: a site makes a film-coated tablet. Keep this list nearby; later lessons refer back to it.
list: MedTech: WI-MD-031 incoming inspection instruction for cuff tubing (Rev C, later Rev D), training record TRN-MD-5520, complaint CMP-MD-1103, nonconformance NC-MD-0417, CAPA-MD-0088, change request CR-MD-0231, supplier file SUP-MD-12.

Pharma: SOP-PH-022 batch record issue and control, master batch record MBR-PH-110 (version 5, later version 6), training record TRN-PH-3304, batch B24-017, deviation DEV-PH-0592, CAPA-PH-0141, change control CC-PH-0310.
Both cases end in a management review where leaders see the trend and the status of the fixes.

p: A controlled document is any document the QMS says must be managed: procedures, work instructions, specifications, drawings, forms and master batch records. Each one moves through the same states. A draft is written by an author. Reviewers check it for accuracy and impact. An approver, often from the quality unit, signs it. It becomes effective on a stated date. When a new version replaces it, the old one is superseded. When the process no longer exists, the document is retired.

The core promise of document control is simple: at the point of use, people can only reach the current approved version. That is harder than it sounds. Printed copies, bookmarks, local downloads and copies pasted into emails all survive after a new version takes effect. Good systems mark printed copies as controlled or uncontrolled, pull superseded copies from the floor, and run periodic reviews so documents do not drift away from how the work is really done.

A new version is not ready for use just because it is approved. The people who do the work must be trained on it first. For drug manufacturing, 21 CFR 211.25 requires that people have the education, training and experience for their job and are trained in the procedures they use. ISO 13485 asks device makers to establish competence and keep records of training.

That is why a training record names the document and its version, not just the topic. When MBR-PH-110 moved from version 5 to version 6, every operator who runs the tablet press needed a training record for version 6 before running a batch. A read-and-understood signature may be enough for a small wording change. A changed setting or a new step usually needs a demonstration or an observed run.
Training also carries quality culture. People who are trained and trusted report problems early, such as a printed copy that looks out of date. People who fear blame hide them.

Documents say what should happen. Records prove what did happen. Good documentation practice (GDP) is the set of habits that keeps records believable: write in permanent ink or a controlled system, record at the time of the work, never use correction fluid or overwrite, and correct an error with a single line, the new value, the date, the initials and a reason.
Regulators summarise these habits as ALCOA+. Every record should be:
list: Attributable: you can tell who did it.
Legible: anyone can read it, now and later.
Contemporaneous: recorded when the work happened.
Original: the first capture, or a verified true copy.
Accurate: correct, with any change traceable.
The plus: complete, consistent, enduring and available for the whole retention period.

p: In the US, 21 CFR Part 11 sets the rules for electronic records and electronic signatures that are used in place of paper under other FDA rules. In practice this means the system is validated for its use, access is limited to authorised people, a secure computer-generated audit trail records who created, changed or deleted data and when, and each electronic signature is linked to its record and shows the signer, the date and time, and the meaning, such as approval or review. In the EU, Annex 11 of the GMP guide covers similar ground for computerised systems.
For an FDE the practical rule is: never build a path that edits a controlled record without going through the system's audit trail, and never let a script sign on behalf of a person.

AI is useful here. It can compare two versions of a procedure and list the changed steps, draft a training summary of what changed, flag documents overdue for periodic review, or find work records that cite a superseded version. It cannot approve a document, decide who needs training or sign a record. A named, trained person still does those, and the tool's output is treated as a draft until they do.

example.title: Worked example: catching a superseded version with a query (example scenario)
p: In the Pharma case, MBR-PH-110 version 6 took effect on an example date. Operator A was trained on version 6. Operator B was trained only on version 5, and a printed version 5 copy was still in the room. Batch B24-017 was run by operator B on version 5 two days after version 6 took effect.

The SQLite script below holds a tiny copy of the three record types and flags any work done on a superseded version or by someone not trained on the version that was current at the time. It runs as written in the sqlite3 shell. The first row is the gap that becomes deviation DEV-PH-0592 in the next lesson.

code.text:
CREATE TABLE doc_version (doc_id TEXT, version TEXT, effective_on TEXT, superseded_on TEXT);
CREATE TABLE training (person TEXT, doc_id TEXT, version TEXT, completed_on TEXT);
CREATE TABLE work_record (record_id TEXT, person TEXT, doc_id TEXT, version_used TEXT, done_on TEXT);
INSERT INTO doc_version VALUES
  ('MBR-PH-110', '5', '2026-01-10', '2026-06-02'),
  ('MBR-PH-110', '6', '2026-06-02', NULL);
INSERT INTO training VALUES
  ('op-A', 'MBR-PH-110', '6', '2026-05-28'),
  ('op-B', 'MBR-PH-110', '5', '2026-01-08');
INSERT INTO work_record VALUES
  ('B24-017', 'op-B', 'MBR-PH-110', '5', '2026-06-04'),
  ('B24-018', 'op-A', 'MBR-PH-110', '6', '2026-06-05');
-- Flag work done on a superseded version or without training on the current version
SELECT w.record_id, w.person, w.version_used,
  CASE WHEN d.superseded_on IS NOT NULL AND w.done_on >= d.superseded_on
       THEN 'superseded version used' ELSE 'version ok' END AS version_check,
  CASE WHEN t.person IS NULL THEN 'not trained on current version'
       ELSE 'trained on current version' END AS training_check
FROM work_record w
JOIN doc_version d ON d.doc_id = w.doc_id AND d.version = w.version_used
JOIN doc_version cur ON cur.doc_id = w.doc_id AND cur.effective_on <= w.done_on
  AND (cur.superseded_on IS NULL OR cur.superseded_on > w.done_on)
LEFT JOIN training t ON t.person = w.person AND t.doc_id = w.doc_id
  AND t.version = cur.version AND t.completed_on <= w.done_on;

practice.title: Build a controlled record set
practice.goal: Hold documents, versions, training and work records in a form you can check for gaps.
steps: Copy the SQLite script from the worked example into a file and run it with sqlite3 to see the two result rows.
Add the MedTech case: WI-MD-031 Rev C and Rev D, an inspector trained on Rev D, and one inspection record done on Rev C after Rev D took effect.

pitfalls: Treating approval as the moment a document can be used. People must be trained on the new version before the effective date, or the go-live must wait.
Leaving printed or downloaded copies in circulation after a revision. Withdraw superseded copies and mark printed copies so their status is clear.
Recording training against a topic rather than a document version. An auditor will ask which version the person was trained on.
Fixing a data error with a direct database update. Corrections must go through the system so the audit trail shows the old value, the new value, who and why.
Letting an AI-drafted procedure go straight to approval. The author and reviewers own the content and must check every step against the real process.

lessons.title: Deviations, complaints and CAPA
lessons.summary: You will be able to trace a quality event from first report to a closed CAPA, tell a correction from a corrective action, and write an effectiveness check that can actually fail.
lessons.why: CAPA is where quality data turns into decisions, so it is one of the first places companies ask for help: search over past investigations, trend dashboards, AI drafts of investigation reports. To build any of these well you need to know what a good investigation looks like, which steps a person must own, and why a weak root cause or a vague effectiveness check is a problem an inspector will find.

p: A quality event is anything that shows a product, process or record may not meet its requirements. The names differ by industry. In medicine manufacturing, a deviation is a departure from an approved instruction or procedure, such as running a step outside the written range. In device manufacturing, a nonconformance is a product or part that does not meet its specification. Both industries handle complaints from customers, findings from audits and inspections, out-of-specification laboratory results, and adverse trends spotted in data.

In the running case, three events enter the QMS. In Pharma, deviation DEV-PH-0592 is opened because batch B24-017 was compressed using version 5 of MBR-PH-110 after version 6 took effect. In MedTech, complaint CMP-MD-1103 reports a cracked air tube on a cuff, and nonconformance NC-MD-0417 later records a tubing lot that failed incoming inspection.

The first job is to stop the problem spreading. For DEV-PH-0592 that means holding batch B24-017 in quarantine so it cannot be released while the deviation is open. For a device complaint it can mean checking whether other units from the same lot are in stock.

Next comes triage. The team assesses the possible impact on the patient and the product and classifies the event using the company's procedure, often as minor, major or critical. Rules apply here. For drugs, 21 CFR 211.192 requires any unexplained discrepancy to be thoroughly investigated, and the investigation must extend to other batches that may be affected. For devices, every complaint must be evaluated, including whether it must be reported to the FDA under the medical device reporting rule in 21 CFR Part 803.

Not every event needs a CAPA. A one-off, well-understood event with a clear correction can be closed in the deviation or complaint record. A CAPA is opened when the cause is systemic, the risk is high, or the event repeats. Each company sets these triggers in its CAPA procedure.

A root cause is the most basic cause that, if removed, would stop the problem from happening again. Common tools are the 5 whys (ask why until you reach a cause the company controls), the fishbone or Ishikawa diagram (sort possible causes into groups such as people, methods, materials, machines, measurement and environment), and fault tree analysis (work down from an event through AND and OR logic to basic causes).

Human error is rarely a root cause on its own. If an operator used the wrong version, ask why the wrong version was within reach and why the training system did not catch it. A finding of 'operator error, retrain' with nothing else is a classic weak investigation.

Every step in the chain needs evidence, not opinion. For DEV-PH-0592 that means the batch record pages actually used, the document system history for MBR-PH-110, the training records for the shift and interviews with the people involved. For CAPA-MD-0088 it means the returned cuffs, test results on aged tubing and the cleaning instructions given to hospitals. When the evidence does not support a cause, say so and keep looking. Record the causes you ruled out as well, with the reason, because a reviewer will ask what else you considered.
These three words are often mixed up. Keep them apart, because an inspector will.
list: Correction: fix the immediate problem, such as reworking or rejecting the affected units, or replacing a cracked cuff for a customer.
Corrective action: remove the cause so the same problem does not happen again, such as changing how batch records are issued.
Preventive action: remove the cause of a potential problem that has not happened yet, such as applying the same fix to the packaging line before it fails there.

p: A CAPA is not closed when the actions are done. It is closed when there is evidence the actions worked. Write the effectiveness check when you plan the actions, not at the end. A good check names a measure, a target, a time window and a data source, and it must be able to fail. 'Monitor for recurrence' is not a check. 'No batch records issued from an uncontrolled printer in the next 50 issues, confirmed by the issue log' is.
If the check fails, the CAPA goes back to investigation. Open, overdue and repeat CAPAs are then trended and reported to management review, which is the subject of a later lesson.

AI tools can group complaints by failure mode, find past deviations with similar descriptions, draft an investigation summary from the record, and suggest fishbone categories to explore. Each output is a hypothesis, not a finding. The investigator must check every claim against the evidence, and a named person still approves the root cause, the actions and the closure.

These tools are only as good as the records behind them. If complaint descriptions are free text with no failure code, or deviations are closed with one-line root causes, a trend tool will group the wrong things. Part of the FDE job is to show the quality team where the data is too thin to support the analysis they want.

The quality unit decides the disposition of B24-017 from the investigation data; the lesson does not assume the outcome.

A fishbone points to materials and measurement: the tube material becomes brittle after repeated wiping with the disinfectant named in the instructions for use, and incoming inspection WI-MD-031 Rev C tests only new tubing. list: Why was B24-017 compressed at the old settings? The operator followed MBR-PH-110 version 5.

Writing effectiveness checks such as 'monitor for recurrence' that cannot fail. Name a measure, a target and a time window.
Investigating only the batch or lot in front of you. Check whether other batches, lots or lines share the same cause.
Pasting an AI-drafted root cause into the record without checking the evidence. The investigator signs for every statement in it.

Hold it in quarantine while the deviation is investigated
Destroy it at once to remove any risk to patients
Ship it and add a note to the batch file for later review

A complaint
A change request
A management review finding

options: Retraining should be done by an outside company
The operator should have been named in the title of the investigation report
It never asks why the wrong version was available to use
The deviation should have been classified as critical
questions.why: Human error is rarely the root cause; the system that allowed the error must be investigated and fixed.

options: Replacing the cracked cuff for the hospital that complained
Rejecting the failed tubing lot at incoming inspection
Reworking the tablets from batch B24-017 if QA allows it
Changing to a tube material that resists the disinfectant
questions.why: A corrective action removes the cause so the problem does not recur; the others fix the immediate units only.

questions.q: After fixing the tablet line, the team applies the same batch record controls to the packaging line, which has had no problem yet. What is this?
options: A correction
A preventive action
A containment step for the line
A deviation
questions.why: Preventive action removes the cause of a potential problem before it happens.

questions.q: Which is the best effectiveness check for CAPA-PH-0141?
options: Monitor batch records closely for any recurrence of the problem over time
QA will review the CAPA again at some point next year
Zero uncontrolled batch record issues in the next 50, per the issue log
The operators confirm they understand the new process well
questions.why: A good check has a measure, a target, a window and a data source, and it can fail.

Only the single batch where the problem was found
The financial cost of the batch to the company
Whether the operator has had a recent annual performance review
questions.why: The rule says the investigation extends to other batches of the same product and other products that may be affected.

Whether the hospital used the right supplier
Whether the complaint can be closed quietly without making a record
Whether it must be reported to the FDA under Part 803

options: Close the CAPA, since the actions were completed
The CAPA goes back to investigation
Delete the two complaints as unrelated
Wait another year before deciding
questions.why: A failed effectiveness check means the root cause or the actions were wrong, so the investigation reopens.

Send it straight to QA approval to save time
Ask the tool a second time and use the newer answer
Check every claim against the evidence and own the result

lessons.title: Change control
lessons.summary: You will be able to say what counts as a controlled change, list what an impact assessment must cover, and explain why a prompt or model update to a quality tool is a change too.
lessons.why: FDEs make changes for a living: a new data feed, a new version of a script, a new prompt. In a regulated company each of those can touch a validated process or a filed product, and making it without change control is one of the fastest ways to create an inspection finding. Knowing the process lets you plan the evidence early instead of having your release blocked at the end.

p: A controlled change is any planned change to something the QMS depends on to keep product quality and patient safety: the product design, materials and suppliers, manufacturing processes and equipment, facilities and utilities, test methods, controlled documents, and the computerised systems used in production and quality. If a change could affect the product, the process or the evidence that they are under control, it goes through change control.

The change owner raises a change request, describes what will change and why, and proposes a plan. Reviewers from the affected areas assess impact. The quality unit approves, and for larger changes a change control board brings the functions together. The goal is not paperwork. It is to make sure nobody is surprised by the consequences of a change after it reaches the product.

In the running case, two changes come out of the CAPAs. CR-MD-0231 changes the cuff tube to a new material from a new supplier. CC-PH-0310 changes how batch records are issued: from local printing to numbered copies issued only by QA from the document system.
The impact assessment is the heart of change control. It asks, area by area, what else this change touches. A useful habit is to go through the same list every time so nothing is skipped:
list: Product quality and safety: could the change affect performance, purity, sterility, shelf life or how the product is used?
Risk: does the product risk file or process risk assessment need updating?
Validation and qualification: do processes, equipment, test methods or software need new testing?
Documents and training: which procedures, specifications, drawings and batch records change, and who must be retrained?
Suppliers and materials: are new suppliers qualified, and do quality agreements cover the change?
Regulatory: does a filing, registration or certificate describe the thing being changed?
Other products and sites: is the same part, material or system used elsewhere?

p: An approved change becomes a plan with tasks, owners and due dates. Effectivity says exactly when the change takes hold: from which lot, batch, serial number or date. Without clear effectivity nobody can tell later which products were made the old way and which the new way, and that matters when a complaint arrives.

Once the tasks are done, the owner shows evidence that the change works as intended, such as test results, a successful first batch or a completed training list, and quality closes the change. Most procedures also allow emergency or temporary changes, but they still need documented approval and a follow-up assessment, never a quiet fix.

Change control and CAPA feed each other. Many corrective actions are carried out as changes, as CR-MD-0231 and CC-PH-0310 are here, and the CAPA cannot pass its effectiveness check until the change is implemented. In the other direction, a change that goes wrong is itself a quality event and may open a deviation. Link the records both ways so an auditor can follow the chain.

sections.h: When the regulator must be told
p: Some changes need the regulator to be told, or to approve, before or after they are made. For approved medicines in the US, 21 CFR 314.70 sorts changes into major changes that need a prior approval supplement, moderate changes reported in a supplement before or at the time of the change, and minor changes reported in the annual report. In the EU, changes to a marketing authorisation are handled as variations of different types. ICH Q12 adds tools that help companies plan and manage post-approval changes.

For devices in the US, FDA guidance helps decide when a change to a cleared device needs a new 510(k). A predetermined change control plan, agreed with the FDA in a marketing submission, can describe certain planned future changes in advance. In the EU, significant changes may need assessment by the notified body.
Deciding the regulatory route is the job of regulatory affairs specialists. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, not the authority to decide.

Software used in production or the QMS is under change control like equipment. For an AI tool that means more than code. A changed prompt, a new model version, a different retrieval index, a new data source or a changed confidence threshold can all change the output. Treat each one as a change: describe it, assess impact, rerun the agreed test set, and record the result before release.

Watch for changes you do not make yourself. A hosted model can be updated by the vendor. Pin model versions where the service allows it, and agree with the quality team how vendor updates will be detected and assessed.

A simple release record helps a lot: for each release, note the prompt version, the model name and version, the date the retrieval index was built, the data sources, and the test set result. With that record, anyone can answer which configuration produced a given output on a given day.

example.title: Worked example: impact assessment for CR-MD-0231 (example scenario)
p: CAPA-MD-0088 found that the cuff tube becomes brittle with the disinfectant named in the instructions for use. The corrective action is to switch to a new tube material from a new supplier. Here is a short impact assessment, area by area. The answers are illustrative; a real one cites the evidence for each line.

For the Pharma case, CC-PH-0310 is smaller but follows the same steps: SOP-PH-022 is revised, the document system is configured so only QA can issue numbered batch record copies, the configuration change is tested, users are trained, and effectivity is set from the first batch after go-live. Its impact on the product filing is assessed as none, which regulatory affairs confirms in the record.
list: Product: tube is a design change, so design verification tests are repeated on cuffs with the new tube, including tests after repeated disinfection.
Risk: the risk file entry for tube cracking is updated with the new control and test evidence.
Validation: the tube assembly process is checked for any setting that depends on the old material.
Documents and training: drawing, material specification and WI-MD-031 move to new revisions; Rev D adds a conditioned hardness test; inspectors are trained (TRN-MD-5520).
Supplier: the new supplier is qualified and added to the approved supplier list with file SUP-MD-12.
Regulatory: regulatory affairs assesses whether the change needs a new submission and records the decision.
Effectivity: from the first cuff lot built with the new tube lot; old-material stock is segregated.

practice.title: Assess a prompt change like an engineer in a QMS
practice.goal: Apply the impact assessment list to a change in an AI tool used in a quality process.
steps: Imagine a tool that drafts complaint summaries for CMP-MD records. The change: a new prompt that also asks the model to suggest a failure code.
Write the change request: what changes, why, and which records the tool touches.
Go through each line of the impact assessment list and write one sentence per area, including 'no impact' with a reason where true.
Write a verification plan: which saved test cases you rerun, what result passes, and who reviews it.
State the effectivity: from which date or version the new prompt applies, and how old summaries stay traceable.

pitfalls: Starting the work before the change is approved because it seems small. Even a small change needs an approved record before it touches the product or a validated system.
Writing 'no impact' without a reason. Each area needs a short justification an auditor can follow.
Leaving effectivity vague. If you cannot say which lot first used the new material, you cannot answer a complaint about it.
Forgetting other products and sites. The same part, material or system is often shared.
Treating a prompt or model update as configuration that needs no review. It can change outputs and must be assessed and tested like code.

An emergency change, documented and assessed after
Stop the whole site until the change board meets

Deleting all old batch records from the archive

Wait for complaints on the other model before acting
Raise a separate change only if the auditor asks
Assess the other model as part of the impact

lessons.title: Audits, supplier oversight and management review
lessons.summary: You will be able to describe how internal and supplier audits work, what a quality agreement is for, and what goes into and comes out of a management review.
lessons.why: Audits and management reviews are where quality data is read by people who make decisions. FDEs are often asked to build the trend reports, supplier scorecards and review packs that feed them. If you know what an auditor samples and what leaders must decide, you can build reports that answer real questions instead of charts that look busy.

p: An internal audit is a planned, independent check that the company follows its own procedures and the rules that apply to it. Independent means auditors do not audit their own work. Both device and medicine quality systems expect a planned audit programme, and the plan is risk based: every QMS process is covered over a cycle, and areas with high risk, recent changes or past problems are audited more often.

An audit has a scope, a plan, an opening meeting, fieldwork and a closing meeting. Fieldwork is mostly sampling and tracing. An auditor picks a record and follows its links: from a batch record to the batch record version, to the operator, to that operator's training record, to the deviation that was raised, to its CAPA and the effectiveness evidence. A finding states the requirement, the evidence seen and the gap between them, so the owner can act on it. Findings are then handled through CAPA.

External audits follow the same pattern. Customers audit their suppliers, notified bodies audit device makers for certification, and regulators inspect. A company that runs honest internal audits and closes the findings is rarely surprised by an external one, because it has already sampled and traced its own records the way an inspector will.

Much of what goes into a product is bought: materials, components, contract manufacturing, testing and software. The company stays responsible for the quality of what it buys. ICH Q10 says this directly for outsourced activities in medicines, and device rules expect purchasing controls in proportion to the risk of the purchased item.

Rules also shape how much a company can rely on a supplier's own test results. For drug components in the US, 21 CFR 211.84 allows a supplier's certificate of analysis to replace some testing only with at least a specific identity test by the company and periodic checks that the supplier's results are reliable. Supplier oversight has four parts:
list: Qualification: before first use, assess the supplier in proportion to risk, using questionnaires, samples, certificates and, for critical suppliers, an on-site or remote audit.
Approved supplier list: only qualified suppliers can be used for a given item, and the list is controlled.

Quality agreement: a written agreement that says who is responsible for which quality activities, such as testing, change notification and handling of deviations. For drugs, FDA guidance describes quality agreements for contract manufacturing.
Monitoring: incoming inspection results, nonconformances, delivery and audit results are trended, and problems go back to the supplier as a supplier corrective action request.

p: Management review is a regular, recorded meeting where top management looks at how the QMS is performing and decides what to do. ISO 13485 requires it for devices, and ICH Q10 names it as one of the four elements of a pharmaceutical quality system. Under the FDA QMSR, management review, internal audit and supplier audit reports are no longer exempt from FDA inspection, so these records must be written knowing an investigator may read them.

Typical inputs are audit results, complaints and customer feedback, CAPA status and effectiveness, process and product performance, changes that could affect the QMS, supplier performance, new or changed regulations, and actions from the previous review. Outputs are decisions: improvements to make, resources to provide and changes to the QMS, each with an owner. A review that lists data but records no decisions has not done its job.

Quality metrics turn many records into a few signals: complaint rate by failure mode, deviations per batch, CAPA age, overdue training, right-first-time batch records, supplier lot acceptance. Trending looks for change over time, not only for a value crossing a limit. Three similar complaints in a quarter can matter more than one large event.

Metrics shape behaviour. If leaders only reward fast CAPA closure, people close CAPAs fast with weak root causes. If deviation counts are punished, people stop reporting. A healthy quality culture rewards early reporting, treats repeat problems as system failures, and has leaders who ask about effectiveness, not just speed. FDA has published material on quality metrics and quality culture for drug manufacturing; the link below is one example.

sections.h: Where AI and FDE tools fit
p: Good targets for tools are the tedious parts: assembling a management review pack from the eQMS, tracing audit samples across linked records, spotting gaps such as a CAPA closed without effectiveness evidence, and summarising supplier history before an audit. The audit judgement, the finding classification and the review decisions stay with qualified people. A tool that writes findings or decisions on its own would move accountability to software, which no auditor will accept.

p: Internal audit, Pharma. An auditor samples batch B24-018 and traces it to MBR-PH-110 version 6, operator A, and training record TRN-PH-3304: all consistent. She then samples CAPA-PH-0141 and finds the effectiveness check is defined, but the batch record issue log it relies on is a spreadsheet with no access control. Finding: the evidence source for the check is not a controlled record. It goes into a new CAPA.

Supplier, MedTech. After CR-MD-0231, the first lots of the new tubing pass, but NC-MD-0417 records a later lot that fails the conditioned hardness test added in WI-MD-031 Rev D. The new control worked: the lot was stopped at incoming inspection. A supplier corrective action request is sent, the supplier's response is filed in SUP-MD-12, and the supplier's monitoring status is raised until results recover.

The leaders record three decisions with owners: fund a controlled batch record issue log, increase incoming testing for the tubing supplier for an agreed period, and audit the packaging line's document practice next quarter.

Holding a management review that presents charts but records no decisions, owners or resources.

The plan is risk based, so problem areas get more
Every area must be audited exactly twice a year
Regulators choose which areas a company audits

options: Managers are never allowed to join audits in any role
Audits must always be done by outside consultants
Auditors should not audit their own work
Production areas are exempt from internal audits

options: Batch records across the tablet area are a mess and need some work
The team seemed unsure about the batch record process during interviews
Training could probably be better in some areas of the plant and offices
SOP-PH-022 requires numbered copies; 2 unnumbered found at press 2

questions.q: A new tubing supplier passed qualification last year. A recent lot failed incoming inspection. What should happen?
options: Send a corrective action request and track their status
Nothing, since the supplier is already qualified
Remove all past lots from finished cuffs immediately
Change the specification so that the failed lot passes inspection

options: To set the price and delivery terms for each order
To state who is responsible for which quality tasks
To transfer all legal responsibility to the supplier
To replace the need to qualify the supplier at all
questions.why: A quality agreement defines quality responsibilities such as testing, change notification and deviations; the owner stays responsible.

questions.q: A management review meeting shows 30 charts and ends with 'noted'. What is missing?
options: More charts with a longer time range
A wet-ink signature from every single attendee in the room
A copy of the previous audit plan
Decisions with owners, resources and due dates
questions.why: Management review outputs are decisions on improvements, resources and QMS changes, each with an owner.

questions.q: Which item is a typical management review input?
options: CAPA status and effectiveness results
The canteen menu for the next month
Personal performance ratings of operators
The marketing launch plan for a new region
questions.why: CAPA status, audits, complaints, process performance, changes and suppliers are standard inputs.

questions.q: Under the FDA QMSR, what changed for device makers about management review and internal audit reports?
options: They no longer need to be written down at all
They must be published on the company website
They are no longer exempt from FDA inspection
They must now be written by an outside auditor
questions.why: The QMSR removed the earlier exemption, so FDA investigators can review these reports.

questions.q: Leaders set a target to close every CAPA within 30 days and reward teams who meet it. What risk does this create?
options: CAPAs will take far longer to close than they did before the target
Fewer complaints will be received from customers
The audit programme will need fewer auditors
Weak root causes and early closure to hit the target
questions.why: Speed-only metrics push teams toward shallow investigations; effectiveness must be measured too.

questions.q: An FDE builds a tool that assembles the management review pack. Which task should stay with people?
options: Pulling CAPA status from the eQMS
Deciding which actions to fund
Counting complaints by failure mode
Listing overdue training records
questions.why: Tools can gather and summarise data; the review decisions and resources are management's accountability.

lessons.title: Device QMS and pharma quality systems side by side
lessons.summary: You will be able to name the main rules for each industry, translate the core QMS words between them, and explain why the same event is handled with different records and reports.
lessons.why: Many FDE engagements cross the line between devices and medicines, and some products are both. A tool built for a pharma deviation process will not fit a device nonconformance process just by renaming fields, and a device team will not trust a tool that talks about batches when they mean lots and serial numbers. Knowing both vocabularies lets you ask the right questions and build the right data model.

p: Both industries run the same core processes from the first lesson: document control, training, problem handling and CAPA, change control, audits and management review. What differs is the rulebook and the emphasis.

For medical devices, ISO 13485 is the international QMS standard. In the US, the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) in 21 CFR Part 820 incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference and took effect on 2 February 2026. Device rules put heavy weight on design controls, because much of a device's safety is decided at the design stage, and on product risk management under ISO 14971.

For medicines, the US rules are the cGMP regulations, such as 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211 for finished drugs. The EU publishes its GMP guide in EudraLex Volume 4. ICH Q10 describes a pharmaceutical quality system across the product lifecycle. Drug rules put heavy weight on manufacturing control, batch records, laboratory testing and an independent quality unit that approves or rejects each batch.
The two industries use risk words differently, and mixing them up causes confusion in meetings.

ISO 14971 is product risk management for devices. It follows a chain from hazard to hazardous situation to harm, estimates the risk, adds controls, verifies them and judges whether the remaining risk is acceptable against the benefit. The result lives in a risk management file that is updated across the product's life.

ICH Q9, revised as Q9(R1), is quality risk management for medicines. It is a general method for assessing, controlling, communicating and reviewing risks to quality across processes, such as deciding how deeply to investigate a deviation or how often to audit a supplier. Device companies also apply risk-based thinking to their QMS processes, but their product risk file follows ISO 14971.

sections.h: The running case in each vocabulary
p: The running case shows the same process steps with different names and records. The list below pairs them. Note that under the QMSR the FDA moved to ISO 13485 terms, so older US device terms such as device master record are being replaced in procedures, though you will still hear them.
list: Unit of production: MedTech tracks lots and often serial numbers; Pharma tracks batches such as B24-017.
Production instructions and record: MedTech uses work instructions such as WI-MD-031 and production records; Pharma uses a master batch record (MBR-PH-110) and an executed batch record.
Problem in production: MedTech raises a nonconformance (NC-MD-0417); Pharma raises a deviation (DEV-PH-0592).

Complaint reporting in the US: device complaints are evaluated for medical device reports under Part 803; for approved drugs, certain quality problems must be sent as field alert reports under 21 CFR 314.81.
Release: a device lot is released after its acceptance activities are complete; a drug batch is approved or rejected by the quality unit, and in the EU certified by a Qualified Person.

Design: device design changes run through design controls and the risk file; drug product and process knowledge comes from pharmaceutical development, and post-approval changes follow the filing rules.

p: Some products are both, such as a prefilled syringe or a drug-coated device. In the US, 21 CFR Part 4 lets the maker of a combination product run one main quality system, either drug cGMP or the device QMS, and add specific provisions from the other. For example, a company running drug cGMP adds the device design control and purchasing requirements that Part 4 lists. If your client makes combination products, ask early which system is the base and which extra provisions apply. The answer changes which records your tool must create and which approvals it must respect.

sections.h: Inspections and what investigators look for
p: Regulators check the system through inspections. In the US, at the end of an inspection an FDA investigator may issue a Form 483 listing observations, and serious or unresolved problems can lead to a warning letter. In the EU, device makers are audited by notified bodies for certification, and medicine sites are inspected by national competent authorities against EU GMP.

Investigators in both industries tend to start where problems are visible: complaints, deviations or nonconformances, CAPA and its effectiveness, change control, and data integrity. They sample a record and trace it through the system, exactly as the internal auditor did in the previous lesson. The response to a 483 and remediation after a warning letter are specialist work; this lesson gives you the vocabulary, not readiness to lead that work.

example.title: Worked example: the same root cause in two industries (example scenario)
p: Suppose the Pharma root cause from DEV-PH-0592, a superseded instruction left at the point of use, had happened on the MedTech line instead. An inspector at a cuff assembly line finds a printed WI-MD-031 Rev C at the bench after Rev D took effect, and one lot inspected to Rev C.

The steps match the Pharma case, but the words, records and reporting questions change. Notice what does not change: contain first, find the system cause, fix it through change control, check effectiveness and report to management review.
list: Event: a nonconformance is raised against the affected tubing lot instead of a deviation against a batch.
Containment: the lot and any cuffs built from it are put on hold; finished cuffs are traced by lot and serial number.
Risk: the team checks the ISO 14971 risk file entry for tube cracking to judge the impact of the missed conditioned test, rather than a Q9 assessment of batch quality.
Release: the affected lot cannot complete acceptance until the missed test is done or the lot is rejected; there is no Qualified Person in the device path.
Reporting: if any complaints follow, they are evaluated under the device reporting rules, not drug field alerts.

practice.title: Build a two-industry glossary for your data model

Add at least ten concepts, starting with the pairs in this lesson: unit of production, production record, problem in production, product release, risk file, reportable event.
For each pair, mark whether one database field could hold both (same meaning) or needs separate fields (different meaning or rules).

pitfalls: Using 'risk management' to mean the same thing in both industries. Say whether you mean ISO 14971 product risk or ICH Q9 quality risk management.
Renaming fields to move a pharma deviation tool to a device team. The records, links and reporting rules differ, not just the labels.
Assuming the FDA QMSR means device makers can ignore FDA-specific requirements. The rule incorporates ISO 13485 and keeps additional FDA requirements.
Forgetting combination products. Ask early which quality system is the base and which extra provisions apply under Part 4.
Treating introductory knowledge of inspections as readiness to manage a 483 response. That work needs specialist quality and regulatory people.

lessons.title: Software and AI inside a QMS
lessons.summary: You will be able to describe what an eQMS holds, explain risk-based assurance of quality software, and write an intended use, approval points and a monitoring plan for an AI tool in a quality process.
lessons.why: This is where the earlier lessons become your daily work. When you put an AI assistant into complaint handling or deviation investigation, the tool itself becomes part of the QMS. It needs an intended use, evidence it works for that use, controls on who decides, records of what it did, and change control when it changes. If you plan these from the first week, the quality team can approve the tool; if you add them at the end, the project usually stalls.

p: An eQMS is the software that holds QMS records: controlled documents and their versions, training assignments and records, complaints, deviations and nonconformances, CAPAs, change controls, audits and supplier files. Its main value is the links between records. In the running case, DEV-PH-0592 links to batch B24-017, to MBR-PH-110, to CAPA-PH-0141 and to CC-PH-0310. A good eQMS lets an auditor follow those links in a few clicks.

Quality data also lives in neighbouring systems: ERP for materials, suppliers and lots; MES or electronic batch records for production; LIMS for laboratory results; PLM for drawings, parts and design changes. Most FDE work on quality is about joining these systems without breaking the controls in any of them.

Keep one distinction clear. Software that is part of a medical device, or is itself a device, is product software and follows device design controls. Software used to make the product or run the QMS, such as an eQMS or an AI triage tool, is production and quality system software. The rules and evidence differ, and a later course covers product software.

sections.h: Assuring software used in quality processes
p: Software used in production or the quality system must be shown to work for its intended use. For device makers, the FDA's computer software assurance guidance describes a risk-based approach: identify the intended use, decide whether a failure could affect product quality or patient safety, focus the most rigorous testing on high-risk functions, and use lighter, less scripted testing where risk is lower. For medicines, GAMP 5 from ISPE is the widely used industry guide for computerised systems, and EU GMP Annex 11 sets EU expectations. Part 11 applies to the electronic records and signatures involved.

Computer system validation and assurance is a specialist discipline. This lesson gives you the ideas so you can plan with the validation team; it does not prepare you to sign off a validation package.

Everything starts with a clear intended use statement. It says what the tool does, for which users, with which inputs, what output it gives, which decision that output supports, and what the tool does not do. The last part matters most. A complaint triage assistant that 'suggests a failure code and lists similar past complaints for a trained complaint specialist, and does not decide reportability' has a narrow, testable scope. One that 'triages complaints' does not.

Once the intended use is written, ask the risk question from the first lesson: if the tool is wrong, what could happen to a patient, a product or a regulatory decision? The answer sets how much testing, review and monitoring the tool needs, and it often shows that the safest design keeps the tool out of the highest-risk decision altogether.

Decide where a person must act before AI output becomes part of a record. Typical approval points are accepting a suggested code, adopting a drafted investigation text, and any decision with regulatory weight, which stays fully human. The reviewer must see the sources the tool used, so they can check rather than trust.

Then record what happened. For each use, log the tool release, model and prompt version, the input record, the output, the reviewer, what the reviewer did with it and the final value. This record lets you answer an auditor's question months later, and it is also your best data for measuring the tool.

The tool must never sign anything. An electronic signature means a named person approves the content, so the screen should mark AI-drafted text clearly, show the reviewer's edits, and require the person's own signature action under the system's Part 11 controls.

An AI tool can get worse without any change on your side: complaint wording shifts, a new product launches, or a vendor updates a model. Plan monitoring before go-live, and when a trigger fires, handle it through the QMS: a quality event record, an assessment, and change control for any fix. Typical monitoring steps:
list: Rerun a fixed, reviewed test set on every change and on a regular schedule.
Track how often reviewers accept, edit or reject suggestions, by product and failure mode.
Sample reviewed outputs for a second check, with more sampling for higher-risk records.
Set triggers that send the tool back to assessment, such as a fall in acceptance or a missed high-risk case.
Watch for automation bias: reviewers who accept everything are not reviewing.

example.title: Worked example: a complaint triage assistant for the MedTech case (example scenario)
p: The MedTech team wants help with complaints like CMP-MD-1103. The intended use: 'For trained complaint specialists, suggest a failure code and list up to five similar past complaints with links, for each new device complaint. The tool does not decide reportability, does not close complaints and does not write to the complaint record without the specialist's action.'

Risk drives the assurance. A wrong failure code is caught by the specialist and costs time. A missed reportable event could harm patients and break the reporting rules, so the tool is kept away from that decision entirely. Testing focuses on whether similar-record search finds known related complaints, using a reviewed set of past complaints.

Each use writes a log entry like the one below. It is valid JSON; the values are invented. A Pharma version of the same tool, searching past deviations for DEV-PH-0592, would need its own intended use and assessment under its own rules, even if the code is shared.

practice.title: Write an AI tool plan the quality team could review
practice.goal: Produce the first four pieces of evidence for an AI tool in a quality process.
steps: Pick the Pharma case: a tool that finds past deviations similar to DEV-PH-0592 and drafts a summary for the investigator.
Write an intended use statement with users, inputs, outputs, the decision it supports and at least two things it does not do.
List the approval points where a person must act, and mark which decisions stay fully human.
Write a log record in JSON for one use, and check it is valid with python3 -m json.tool.
Write a monitoring plan with a test set, two measures and one trigger that sends the tool back to assessment.
practice.done_when: You have an intended use with two explicit exclusions, a list of approval points, a JSON log that passes json.tool, and a monitoring plan with a named trigger.

pitfalls: Writing a broad intended use such as 'helps with complaints'. A vague scope cannot be tested or approved.
Letting AI output be saved into a quality record without a person's action. Every accepted suggestion needs a named reviewer.
Logging the output but not the model, prompt and tool release. Without them you cannot explain or reproduce a past result.
Assuming one validation at go-live is enough. Inputs and vendor models change, so monitoring and periodic review are needed.
Reusing a MedTech assessment for a Pharma deployment of the same code. Each use needs its own intended use and rules.

A colourful dashboard home page
Unlimited file storage space
Automatic closing of old records

options: The firmware running inside an infusion pump at the bedside
An app that is itself a medical device
An AI tool that triages complaints in the eQMS
The display software on a glucose meter
questions.why: A tool used to run the QMS is quality system software; the others are part of, or are, the device.

questions.q: Under a risk-based assurance approach, where should the most rigorous testing go?
options: Equally across every screen and button
On functions whose failure could affect quality or safety
Only on the login page and the user permission settings screens
On whatever the vendor tested least
questions.why: Risk-based assurance focuses effort on high-risk functions and uses lighter testing for low-risk ones.

questions.q: Which intended use statement is the strongest?
options: Helps the quality team with complaints
Uses AI to make complaint handling across the company faster and better overall
Triages all complaints automatically for the company
Suggests a failure code for specialists; does not decide reportability
questions.why: A strong statement names users, output and decision supported, and says what the tool does not do.

questions.q: The triage tool could mark a complaint as not reportable. Why does the example keep it away from that decision?
options: A missed reportable event could harm patients and break rules
Reportability decisions are far too slow and complex for any software to make
Regulators ban all software in complaint handling
The model is not able to read complaint text at all
questions.why: High-risk decisions with regulatory weight stay fully human; the tool supports lower-risk steps.

questions.q: A reviewer accepts an AI-suggested failure code. What must the record show?
options: Only the final code, so that the record stays short and simple to read
The AI tool's name as the approver of the code
The suggestion, the reviewer and what they did with it
Nothing extra, as long as the code is correct
questions.why: The audit trail must show what the tool suggested, who reviewed it and the final decision.

questions.q: Six months after go-live, nobody can say which prompt produced an old summary. What was missing from the log?
options: The reviewer's full email signature block and job title
The colour theme of the user interface
The number of users online at the time
Tool release, model and prompt version
questions.why: Logging the configuration with each use is what makes a past output explainable and reproducible.

questions.q: Reviewers have accepted 100 percent of AI suggestions for three months, including two later found wrong. What does this suggest?
options: The tool is perfect and review can stop
Possible automation bias in the review
The test set should be deleted
The tool should now sign records itself
questions.why: Accepting everything, including wrong suggestions, is a sign reviewers are trusting rather than checking.

questions.q: The same similarity-search code will be used for MedTech complaints and Pharma deviations. What is needed?
options: One shared assessment, since the underlying code is exactly the same
No assessment, since search tools are low risk
Only a vendor certificate for the AI model used
A separate intended use and assessment for each use
questions.why: Different uses carry different risks and rules, so each needs its own intended use and assurance.

questions.q: After an FDE course on CSA and GAMP, what is a fair claim about your role in validation?
options: You can plan with the validation team using the right ideas
You can sign off the full validation package for the client yourself
You can replace the validation team on small projects
You no longer need the quality unit for software
questions.why: Introductory coverage helps you plan and collaborate; validation sign-off is specialist and quality-owned.
